cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 1(a): The (fictitious) Directive (EU) 2025/88 on the security of short-term accommodation, adopted to combat terrorism and serious crime, requires the Member States to ensure that providers of short-term holiday rentals record the identity and the dates of stay of every guest and transmit them to the police. It leaves it to the Member States to decide how long the police may keep the data. Austria transposes it by the (fictitious) Guest Data Act: the police keep the data of all guests for ten years, and any police officer may consult them for the investigation of any offence, without prior authorisation by a court or an independent body. Marta, a Slovenian national who lets holiday flats in Graz, must transmit her guests' data under the Act. She argues that the Act infringes Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights. Austria replies that the Charter does not bind it here: the Act is an Austrian statute, and the ten-year period is a purely national choice that the directive left open. Is the Charter applicable? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. By transposing Directive 2025/88, Austria is 'implementing Union law' within Art 51(1) Charter, and that includes the ten-year period it chose within the discretion the directive leaves it.
• Rule: the Charter always binds the Union's institutions and bodies, but binds the Member States 'only when they are implementing Union law' (Art 51(1)). The Court reads this as every situation governed by EU law (Åkerberg Fransson, C-617/10). Transposing a directive is the classic case.
• Discretion: a Member State that uses a discretion conferred by an EU act still acts within the scope of EU law (N.S., C-411/10); national retention and access rules adopted under an option in a directive are judged against the Charter (Tele2 Sverige, C-203/15). That the Act is an Austrian statute is irrelevant, and so is Marta's nationality: the link to EU law is the directive, not a cross-border element. Art 51(2) Charter does not help Austria, because the directive already governs the matter.
• Consequence: Austrian courts must review the Act against Arts 7 and 8 Charter. Because the directive leaves discretion, Austrian fundamental rights also apply, provided the Charter's level of protection and the primacy of EU law are not compromised (Art 53 Charter; Melloni, C-399/11).
Codex: Art 51(1)–(2), Art 53 Charter; Art 6(1) TEU; Art 288(3) TFEU · Cases: Åkerberg Fransson (C-617/10), N.S. (C-411/10), Tele2 Sverige (C-203/15), Melloni (C-399/11).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 1(b): Karl, an Austrian journalist, is convicted under the Austrian Criminal Code of defaming the mayor of his home town in an article in a local Austrian newspaper. On appeal he invokes the freedom of expression guaranteed by Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights. Can he rely on the Charter? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. Domestic criminal defamation proceedings do not implement Union law, so the Charter does not apply (Art 51(1)); Karl can rely only on Austrian constitutional rights and Art 10 ECHR, which has constitutional rank in Austria.
• The Charter binds the Member States only within the scope of EU law and does not extend that scope (Art 51(2); Art 6(1) TEU). There must be a link of a certain degree with EU law, more than a closely related subject or an indirect impact (Siragusa, C-206/12). Austrian criminal defamation law has no such link; the EU anti-SLAPP Directive 2024/1069 covers only civil and commercial matters with cross-border implications. On a reference, the Court of Justice would have no jurisdiction, because the Charter cannot by itself found it (Åkerberg Fransson, C-617/10).
Codex: Art 51(1)–(2) Charter; Art 6(1) TEU · Cases: Åkerberg Fransson (C-617/10), Siragusa (C-206/12).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 1(c): Marta, a Slovenian national who lets holiday flats in Graz, employs Petra, an Austrian, as a cleaner under a private employment contract. Petra resigns in the middle of the year. Ten days of her paid annual leave for that year, all within the four-week minimum guaranteed by EU law, are still untaken, because Marta never let her take them. Under the (fictitious) Austrian Holiday Act, untaken leave for the current year lapses without any allowance in lieu if the worker resigns. Article 7 of the Working Time Directive 2003/88, which Austria has transposed, gives every worker at least four weeks of paid annual leave, which may not be replaced by an allowance in lieu except where the employment relationship is terminated. Petra sues Marta for an allowance in lieu and invokes Article 31(2) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights. Can she rely on the Charter against Marta, a private person? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. The Holiday Act falls within the scope of Directive 2003/88, so the Charter applies, and although the directive cannot be invoked against a private employer, Art 31(2) Charter is mandatory and unconditional and binds Marta too, so the court must disapply the Austrian rule (Bauer, C-569/16 and C-570/16; Max-Planck, C-684/16).
• Scope: national rules on paid annual leave implement Art 7 of the directive (Art 51(1)); no cross-border element is needed, so it does not matter that Petra is Austrian.
• Routes in order: first, consistent interpretation of the Holiday Act. If that would be contra legem, the directive does not help, because directives have no horizontal direct effect (Faccini Dori, C-91/92). Art 31(2) Charter does: it confers by itself a right that a worker may invoke against a private employer, and Art 51(1) does not systematically exclude obligations for private parties (Bauer; Egenberger, C-414/16).
• Merits: the allowance in lieu is due whenever the employment relationship ends, even if the worker resigns early without good cause (job-medium, C-233/20, on the Austrian Urlaubsgesetz). Leave may lapse only if the employer actually enabled the worker to take it, which Marta did not (Max-Planck).
• Limit: not every Charter provision works horizontally; Art 27 does not (AMS, C-176/12).
Codex: Arts 27, 31(2), 51(1) Charter; Art 288(3) TFEU; Directive 2003/88, Art 7 · Cases: Bauer (C-569/16 and C-570/16), Max-Planck (C-684/16), job-medium (C-233/20), Egenberger (C-414/16), AMS (C-176/12), Faccini Dori (C-91/92).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 2(a): The (fictitious) Directive (EU) 2025/88 on the security of short-term accommodation, adopted to combat terrorism and serious crime, requires the Member States to ensure that providers of short-term holiday rentals record the identity and the dates of stay of every guest and transmit them to the police. It leaves it to the Member States to decide how long the police may keep the data. Austria transposes it by the (fictitious) Guest Data Act: the police keep the data of all guests for ten years, and any police officer may consult them for the investigation of any offence, without prior authorisation by a court or an independent body. Assume that the Charter of Fundamental Rights applies. Is this regime a justified limitation of Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter? Examine the conditions of Article 52(1) of the Charter. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. The Act is provided for by law, respects the essence of Arts 7 and 8 Charter and pursues an objective of general interest, but keeping every guest's data for ten years, with access for any offence and without prior review, goes beyond what is strictly necessary.
• Interference: storing all guests' data and giving the police access limits private life (Art 7) and data protection (Art 8) (Digital Rights Ireland, C-293/12 and C-594/12).
• Art 52(1) test: (1) provided for by law: yes, a statute. (2) Essence: not affected, because only identity and dates of stay are kept, which do not give a full picture of private life. (3) Objective of general interest recognised by the Union: fighting terrorism and serious crime, yes. (4) Proportionality: suitable, but limitations of data protection must be confined to what is strictly necessary.
• Application of (4): the Act covers every guest without any link to a threat, keeps the data for ten years without differentiation, and opens access to any officer for any offence, beyond the aim of fighting serious crime, without prior review by a court or an independent body (Digital Rights Ireland; Tele2 Sverige, C-203/15). For the travel data of all air passengers the Court accepted general retention only for six months, after which data may be kept only where there is objective evidence of a risk (Ligue des droits humains, C-817/19). A short general period and access only for serious crime with prior review would restrict less.
• Result: Arts 7 and 8 are infringed. Austrian courts must disapply the offending provisions; they may refer under Art 267 TFEU, and a court of last instance must unless a CILFIT exception applies.
Codex: Arts 7, 8, 52(1) Charter; Art 267 TFEU · Cases: Digital Rights Ireland (C-293/12 and C-594/12), Tele2 Sverige (C-203/15), Ligue des droits humains (C-817/19), CILFIT (283/81).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 2(b): Austria's (fictitious) Guest Data Act, which transposes an EU directive, lets the police keep the data of all holiday guests for ten years. Before the Austrian courts Austria argues that Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights can never give more protection than Article 8 ECHR as interpreted by the European Court of Human Rights. Is this correct? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. Under Art 52(3) Charter, rights that correspond to ECHR rights have the same meaning and scope as in the Convention, but this 'shall not prevent Union law providing more extensive protection'. The ECHR is a floor, not a ceiling.
• Art 53 Charter: the Charter may not be interpreted as restricting rights recognised by the ECHR or the national constitutions. Art 8 Charter (data protection) has no express counterpart in the ECHR's text. The ECHR is not formally part of EU law while the EU has not acceded (Art 6(2)–(3) TEU; Opinion 2/13).
Codex: Arts 52(3), 53 Charter; Art 6(2)–(3) TEU · Cases: Opinion 2/13.

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 3(a): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Give reasons. 'Because regulations are directly applicable (Article 288(2) TFEU), every provision of a regulation has direct effect.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: False. Direct applicability and direct effect are different concepts. A provision of a regulation has direct effect only if it is clear, precise and unconditional and confers rights or obligations on individuals.
• Direct applicability: a regulation is part of national law automatically, without any national measure of reception (Variola, 34/73).
• Direct effect: the individual can invoke the provision in court. Regulations are by nature capable of it, vertically and horizontally (Politi, 43/71; Muñoz, C-253/00). A provision that leaves the Member States discretion or needs national implementing measures cannot be relied on (Monte Arcosu, C-403/98).
Codex: Art 288(2) TFEU · Cases: Van Gend en Loos (26/62), Variola (34/73), Politi (43/71), Muñoz (C-253/00), Monte Arcosu (C-403/98).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 3(b): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Give reasons. 'Mrs Horvat bought a vacuum cleaner from the door-to-door salesman of a private company. A (fictitious) consumer directive gives buyers a 14-day right to cancel such contracts. Austria has not transposed it, although the transposition deadline has expired. Mrs Horvat can rely on the directive against the company to cancel the contract.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: False. Even a clear, precise and unconditional provision of a directive has no horizontal direct effect, so it cannot be invoked against a private company (Marshall I, 152/84; Faccini Dori, C-91/92).
• Reasons: a directive binds only the Member States to which it is addressed (Art 288(3) TFEU), and the estoppel rationale of vertical direct effect does not reach private parties.
• Workarounds: consistent interpretation of Austrian law as far as possible, but not contra legem (Von Colson, 14/83; Marleasing, C-106/89). Failing that, Francovich damages from Austria; non-transposition is in itself a sufficiently serious breach (Dillenkofer, C-178/94).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 288(3) TFEU · Cases: Marshall I (152/84), Faccini Dori (C-91/92), Von Colson (14/83), Marleasing (C-106/89), Francovich (C-6/90 and C-9/90), Dillenkofer (C-178/94).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 3(c): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Give reasons. 'Not only Austrian courts but also Austrian administrative authorities must disapply an Austrian statute that conflicts with directly effective EU law.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: True. Primacy binds all organs of the state. Administrative authorities, including municipal ones, must apply directly effective EU law and refrain from applying conflicting national provisions (Fratelli Costanzo, 103/88).
• Basis: primacy (Costa v ENEL, 6/64; Simmenthal, 106/77) and sincere cooperation (Art 4(3) TEU). It binds even a national competition authority (CIF, C-198/01).
• Limits: an authority cannot itself refer to the Court of Justice, because only a 'court or tribunal' may (Art 267 TFEU), and the disapplied statute is not annulled.
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 267 TFEU; Declaration No 17 · Cases: Costa v ENEL (6/64), Simmenthal (106/77), Fratelli Costanzo (103/88), CIF (C-198/01).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 3(d): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Give reasons. 'According to the Court of Justice, EU law takes precedence even over the constitution of a Member State.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: True, from the Court of Justice's perspective: all EU law prevails over all national law, constitutional law included, and the validity of an EU measure cannot be affected by allegations that it breaches fundamental rights or principles of a national constitution (Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, 11/70; Costa v ENEL, 6/64).
• Primacy is judge-made; the Treaties have no express provision, and Declaration No 17 only recalls the case law. The Union respects national identity (Art 4(2) TEU), but the Court of Justice defines its limits.
• National constitutional courts accept primacy only within limits (integration-proof core): Solange I and II, Maastricht, Honeywell, PSPP (2020). In Austria a widely held view reserves the leading principles (Baugesetze) of the Federal Constitution.
Codex: Art 4(2)–(3) TEU; Declaration No 17 · Cases: Costa v ENEL (6/64), Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70); BVerfG Solange I (1974), Solange II (1986), Maastricht (1993), Honeywell (2010), PSPP (2020).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 3(e): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Give reasons. 'Once the Court of Justice has held that a national provision is incompatible with EU law, that provision is void and can no longer be applied in any case.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: False. Primacy means disapplication, not invalidity: the conflicting national rule does not become non-existent, it is set aside in the cases that EU law governs (IN.CO.GE.'90, C-10/97 to C-22/97).
• In a preliminary ruling the Court only interprets EU law and the national court draws the consequences; an infringement judgment is merely declaratory (Art 260(1) TFEU). Either way, the rule still applies to situations outside the scope of EU law, e.g. purely internal ones.
• For legal certainty the Member State must still amend or repeal it (Commission v France, 167/73), or face infringement proceedings and financial penalties (Arts 258, 260(2) TFEU).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Arts 258, 260, 267 TFEU · Cases: Simmenthal (106/77), IN.CO.GE.'90 (C-10/97 to C-22/97), Commission v France (167/73).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 4(a): Case exercise. The (fictitious) Tyrolean Mountain Guides Act 2025 provides that only members of the Tyrolean Mountain Guides Association (the Association) may guide clients for remuneration on Tyrolean glaciers. Membership requires (i) the Austrian state mountain-guide diploma or a foreign diploma recognised as equivalent, and (ii) residence in Tyrol during the two preceding years. The Association is a private association; most of its members are self-employed guides. Tyrol defends the Act on the ground that glacier tours are dangerous and that guides must know the local terrain and the Tyrolean mountain-rescue system. Three persons are concerned. Jana, a Czech mountain guide with a Czech state diploma, lives and works in Brno; every winter she takes groups of Czech clients, for a fee, to the Stubai Glacier for about three weeks. Tomasz, a Polish mountain guide, wants to move to Innsbruck and open his own mountain-guide school there. Luca, an Italian with a recognised Italian diploma, has lived in Innsbruck for three years and wants to take a salaried job as a guide with Alpin GmbH, a private mountain-sports company. Which fundamental freedom is relevant for each of Jana, Tomasz and Luca? Name the Treaty provisions and the facts that point to each. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Jana: freedom to provide services (Arts 56–57 TFEU). Tomasz: freedom of establishment (Art 49 TFEU). Luca: free movement of workers (Art 45 TFEU).
• Jana: she is self-employed and established in the Czech Republic. She guides clients in Austria for a fee, only about three weeks a year and without a fixed base there. Whether an activity is temporary depends on its duration, regularity, periodicity and continuity (Gebhard, C-55/94), and a service may be provided repeatedly over several years (Schnitzer, C-215/01), so a recurring seasonal activity remains a service. Services are residual (Art 57(1)), and Art 57(3) lets the provider pursue the activity temporarily in the host state.
• Tomasz: he is self-employed and wants to move and set up his own school in Innsbruck. That is stable and continuous participation in the economic life of another Member State, for an indefinite period, through a fixed establishment (Art 49(2); Gebhard; Factortame II, C-221/89).
• Luca: he will work for and under the direction of Alpin GmbH in return for remuneration, so he is a worker in the EU sense (Lawrie-Blum, 66/85). Without subordination, Art 49 or Art 56 would apply instead.
• All three are nationals of Member States, and each situation has a cross-border element, so none is purely internal.
Codex: Arts 45, 49, 56, 57 TFEU · Cases: Gebhard (C-55/94), Schnitzer (C-215/01), Factortame II (C-221/89), Lawrie-Blum (66/85).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 4(b): Case exercise. The (fictitious) Tyrolean Mountain Guides Act 2025 provides that only members of the Tyrolean Mountain Guides Association (the Association) may guide clients for remuneration on Tyrolean glaciers. Membership requires (i) the Austrian state mountain-guide diploma or a foreign diploma recognised as equivalent, and (ii) residence in Tyrol during the two preceding years. The Association is a private association; most of its members are self-employed guides. Jana, a Czech mountain guide with a Czech state diploma, lives and works in Brno; every winter she takes groups of Czech clients, for a fee, to the Stubai Glacier in Tyrol for about three weeks. She cannot become a member because she does not live in Tyrol. Tyrol argues that EU law does not apply to her at all, since Jana and all her clients are Czech. Does the Act restrict Jana's fundamental freedom? Examine the scope of the freedom and the type of restriction. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. Art 56 TFEU applies even though Jana and her clients are Czech, and the Act restricts it: the two-year residence condition is indirect discrimination on grounds of nationality that, for a service provider, comes close to denying the freedom altogether, and compulsory membership is a further obstacle.
• Secondary law first: Directive 2005/36, Title II, governs temporary services in regulated professions. A provider legally established in another Member State may not be restricted for reasons relating to qualifications (Art 5(1)) and is exempt from membership of a professional body, subject at most to automatic temporary registration (Art 6(a)); the host state may require a prior declaration (Art 7(1)) and, for safety-relevant professions, a check of qualifications (Art 7(4)). Compulsory membership therefore breaches the directive; the residence condition is not a qualification rule and is examined under Art 56.
• Scope: Art 56 covers services provided in a Member State other than the provider's. A guide who travels with a group from her home state to provide paid services in another is covered (Commission v France, tourist guides, C-154/89), so Tyrol's objection fails.
• Restriction: Art 56 catches discrimination and any measure that prohibits, impedes or renders less attractive the activities of a provider established elsewhere (Säger, C-76/90). Residence in Tyrol is far more easily met by Austrians: indirect discrimination. A residence requirement can deprive the freedom of all useful effect (Van Binsbergen, 33/74), and compulsory membership imposes conditions of establishment on a temporary provider.
Codex: Arts 56, 57 TFEU; Directive 2005/36, Arts 5–7 · Cases: Commission v France (C-154/89), Säger (C-76/90), Van Binsbergen (33/74).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 4(c): Case exercise. The (fictitious) Tyrolean Mountain Guides Act 2025 provides that only members of the Tyrolean Mountain Guides Association may guide clients for remuneration on Tyrolean glaciers. Membership requires (i) the Austrian state mountain-guide diploma or a foreign diploma recognised as equivalent, and (ii) residence in Tyrol during the two preceding years. Jana, a Czech mountain guide with a Czech state diploma, lives and works in Brno; every winter she takes groups of Czech clients, for a fee, to the Stubai Glacier for about three weeks, and she cannot become a member. Assume that the Act restricts her freedom to provide services. Tyrol argues that glacier tours are dangerous and that guides must know the local terrain and the Tyrolean mountain-rescue system. Can the restriction be justified? Examine the grounds of justification and proportionality. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. Client safety is an overriding reason in the public interest, but neither the residence requirement nor compulsory membership is suitable and necessary to achieve it, because less restrictive means exist.
• Grounds: the written grounds (Art 62 with Art 52(1) TFEU: public policy, public security, public health) require a genuine and sufficiently serious threat to a fundamental interest of society and do not really fit. Since the Act is not directly discriminatory, unwritten overriding reasons are also available: protection of service recipients and safety in the mountains (Säger, C-76/90; Gebhard, C-55/94).
• Suitability: residence does not prove knowledge of the glaciers. A guide who has lived in Innsbruck for two years may never have been on the Stubai Glacier, while Jana has guided there every winter, so the aim is not pursued in a consistent and systematic manner (Hartlauer, C-169/07).
• Necessity: Tyrol could require a prior declaration and check Jana's qualifications before her first service, with an aptitude test only if substantial differences would endanger safety (Directive 2005/36, Art 7(4)), plus a briefing on the rescue system or proof of insurance. It must take account of requirements Jana already meets in her home state (Säger). Membership must give way to automatic temporary registration (Art 6(a)). Likewise, a licence requirement for tourist guides travelling with groups was held disproportionate (Commission v France, C-154/89).
• The burden of proof lies with Austria. Result: Art 56 TFEU and the directive are infringed.
Codex: Arts 52(1), 56, 62 TFEU; Directive 2005/36, Arts 6(a), 7(4) · Cases: Säger (C-76/90), Gebhard (C-55/94), Hartlauer (C-169/07), Commission v France (C-154/89).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 4(d): Case exercise. The (fictitious) Tyrolean Mountain Guides Act 2025 allows only members of the Tyrolean Mountain Guides Association to guide clients for remuneration on Tyrolean glaciers, and membership requires two years' residence in Tyrol. Jana, a Czech mountain guide established in Brno, guides Czech clients for a fee on the Stubai Glacier for three weeks every winter without being a member. Assume that the residence and membership requirements infringe Article 56 TFEU. The district authority (Bezirkshauptmannschaft) fines Jana EUR 2,000. She appeals to the Tyrolean Regional Administrative Court (Landesverwaltungsgericht Tirol), whose decisions can be challenged before the Austrian Supreme Administrative Court (VwGH) and the Constitutional Court (VfGH). The Regional Administrative Court believes that only the VfGH can set aside a statute. How must it proceed, and may or must it refer questions to the Court of Justice? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: It must itself disapply the residence and membership requirements, which conflict with directly effective Art 56 TFEU, and annul the fine, without waiting for the VfGH. It may refer to the Court of Justice (Art 267(2)) but is not obliged to, because its decisions can be challenged.
• Direct effect and primacy: Art 56 is a clear, precise and unconditional prohibition that individuals can invoke against the state (Van Binsbergen, 33/74). Every national court must, of its own motion, set aside conflicting national law without awaiting its removal by legislative or constitutional means (Simmenthal, 106/77). A priority constitutional review is acceptable only if the court stays free to refer and to disapply (Melki and Abdeli, C-188/10 and C-189/10). The district authority should already have disapplied the Act (Fratelli Costanzo, 103/88).
• Art 267: its decisions can be challenged before the VwGH, even if the appeal needs admission, so it is not a court of last instance (Lyckeskog, C-99/00). The VwGH must refer unless a CILFIT exception applies (Art 267(3); CILFIT, 283/81); after the tourist-guide case law it may be acte éclairé.
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Arts 56, 267(2)–(3) TFEU · Cases: Van Binsbergen (33/74), Simmenthal (106/77), Melki and Abdeli (C-188/10 and C-189/10), Fratelli Costanzo (103/88), Lyckeskog (C-99/00), CILFIT (283/81).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 4(e): Case exercise. The (fictitious) Tyrolean Mountain Guides Act 2025 allows only members of the Tyrolean Mountain Guides Association to guide clients on Tyrolean glaciers. Luca, an Italian with an Italian mountain-guide diploma recognised in Austria as equivalent, has lived in Innsbruck for three years and is a member of the Association. He takes a salaried job as a guide with Alpin GmbH, a private mountain-sports company in Innsbruck. Alpin's internal pay policy grants a 15% 'local training bonus' only to guides who obtained their diploma at the Tyrolean state guide academy, and Luca is refused the bonus. Can Luca rely on EU law against Alpin GmbH? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. Art 45 TFEU has direct effect also against private employers (Angonese, C-281/98). The bonus criterion is unjustified indirect discrimination on grounds of nationality, so Luca can claim the bonus before the Austrian labour court.
• Art 45(2) abolishes any discrimination based on nationality as regards employment, remuneration and other conditions of work. It binds private persons too, because working conditions are also set by individual and collective agreements (Walrave, 36/74; Bosman, C-415/93; Angonese: a private bank required a language certificate obtainable only in Bolzano).
• Restriction: a diploma obtained in Tyrol is a criterion mainly met by Austrians, so it is indirect discrimination (O'Flynn, C-237/94).
• Justification: only objective considerations independent of nationality, applied proportionately. Luca's diploma is recognised as equivalent, so the bonus rewards the place of training, not competence.
• Secondary law: Reg 492/2011, Art 7(1) (equal pay) and Art 7(4) (discriminatory clauses in agreements and collective regulations are void).
Codex: Art 45(1)–(3) TFEU; Reg 492/2011, Art 7(1), (4) · Cases: Angonese (C-281/98), Walrave (36/74), Bosman (C-415/93), O'Flynn (C-237/94).

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 4(f): Case exercise. The (fictitious) Tyrolean Mountain Guides Act 2025 allows only members of the Tyrolean Mountain Guides Association (the Association) to guide clients for remuneration on Tyrolean glaciers. The Association is a private association; most of its members are self-employed guides, and many of its members' clients come from other Member States. In 2026 its general assembly, on its own initiative, adopts a binding 'fair tariff': members must charge at least EUR 480 per guided glacier day. Members who charge less are expelled, which means that under the Act they may no longer guide on glaciers. The Tyrolean government neither required nor approved the tariff. Is the tariff compatible with EU competition law? Which provision is relevant, and what are the consequences of an infringement? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. The tariff is a decision by an association of undertakings fixing minimum prices, a restriction by object under Art 101(1)(a) TFEU that does not meet Art 101(3); it is automatically void (Art 101(2)) and can lead to fines and damages. Art 102, which requires a dominant position and its abuse, is not the provision for price coordination between independent guides.
• Undertakings: self-employed guides offer services on a market, so each is an undertaking (Höfner and Elser, C-41/90; Pavlov, C-180/98); salaried guides are not (Becu, C-22/98). The binding resolution is a decision by an association of undertakings (Wouters, C-309/99). Tyrol neither required nor approved it, so it is the Association's own conduct (contrast Arduino, C-35/99).
• Restriction: price-fixing is listed in Art 101(1)(a) and restricts by object, so effects need not be shown; a by-object restriction that may affect trade is appreciable (Expedia, C-226/11). Trade between Member States: many clients come from other Member States, and the tariff also binds guides from other Member States established in Tyrol.
• No exemption: Art 101(3) fails (no fair share for consumers; minimum prices are not indispensable for safety, which qualification rules ensure). The Wouters/Meca-Medina reasoning does not cover by-object restrictions (European Superleague, C-333/21).
• Consequences: void ex tunc (Art 101(2)), so members cannot lawfully be expelled for undercutting it. Fines by the Commission, for an association up to 10% of the turnover of its members active on the market (Art 23(2) Reg 1/2003), or by the Austrian authorities applying Art 101 (Arts 3, 5 Reg 1/2003; in Austria the Cartel Court, on application of the Federal Competition Authority). Art 101 has horizontal direct effect (BRT v SABAM, 127/73), so expelled guides and clients can claim damages in national courts (Courage v Crehan, C-453/99; Directive 2014/104).
